items.title: Bernard Steinau Interview, 1978-08-02
items.q: But a number of other musicians, including Sharky, Lester Bouchon, Chink Martin, Monk Hazel, Frank Federico.

ctx.x: I was, I was 20 and 21, and I'm finishing my pre-med studies. And my family was in New Orleans. And I would try very hard, both to catch Roger Wolfe's jazz show on WDSU, which I think was on Friday nights, may have been Saturdays. And also, sometimes, to go to jazz club meetings. Because the New Orleans jazz club, I think, started in 47. Might have been 46, but it was around that time. There were a couple of abortive initial attempts. And also, to go to the Parisian Room concerts, which were down in the 100 block…

I think he died in 49. That was before, he died before I came to New Orleans in 49. In any case, but he'd been around for many, many years and in and out of town, of course, too. So he had a reputation. Yeah,

items.title: Bernard Steinau Interview, 1978-07-31
items.q: Cherokee in 1947 at the I think at the Parisian room concerts and at first I found it very very interesting

ctx.x: Street yeah but I can remember that just incidentally we were talking about it and I remember for the record that Lester Bouchon had some sort of operation or else he was sick in any case he was out for a long time and Raymond Burke was substituting or I meant must have been in September 1949 when I arrived uh today and what went on before you know I don't I don't remember I remember when Bouchon came back but uh well you know I I started listening to

Cherokee in 1947 at the I think at the Parisian room concerts and at first I found it very very interesting and very exciting but when they moved into a steady job on Bourbon Street for one thing it got very crowded for another uh they were playing the same thing over and over again and very perfunctorily and I started losing interest in that particular group and didn't go back and I suspect probably that this is the time that Bouchon dropped out and I hadn't heard of Raymond Burke at the time so I really…

well the reason I think we probably were aware of Raymond at least in my case was that uh Orrin Blackstone had told me about him because Raymond was on the very first issue of playback magazine which Orrin put out now you may never have seen that issue no I didn't see the Raymond Raymond you know he yeah Orrin was very interested in Raymond and uh felt that he was one of the unsung heroes and we had that record of slow blues around that Raymond put out himself

items.q: Well you know, you listen to his old, to his records from the 30s, and some of them are extremely good.

ctx.x: and sometimes did play exceptional jazz. Oh yeah, I've enjoyed Shockey more sometimes than others. So I just thought it was terrific when he was really playing.
Well you know, you listen to his old, to his records from the 30s, and some of them are extremely good. Oh, the 20s, yeah. But I mean this is in the 50s. Yeah, I know that.

I'm talking about when I would really enjoy him sometimes when he, well, I think every musician can can get in a rut, black or white, if he's playing on Bourbon Street especially, because I feel the pressure is on them there to be in a rut.
